blocks.content: Tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies governed by the principles of Natural Justice rather than the strict procedural rules of ordinary courts.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Tribunals were incorporated into the Indian Constitution via the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976 based on the Swaran Singh Committee recommendations.
Part XIV-A contains Article 323A (Administrative Tribunals) and Article 323B (Tribunals for other matters like Taxation, Foreign Exchange, and Land Reforms).
Tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies exempted from the strict procedural constraints of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) and Evidence Act, guided instead by Natural Justice.
Following the landmark L. Chandra Kumar case (1997), decisions of tribunals are subject to judicial review under the writ jurisdiction of the Division Bench of High Courts.

rows: Specific matters like Tax, Foreign Exchange, Land Reforms
Created by Parliament or State Legislatures
No provision for hierarchy of tribunals
Hierarchy of tribunals can be created

items: Article 323A allows tribunal creation exclusively by Parliament, whereas Article 323B allows both Parliament and State Legislatures to establish tribunals.
Swaran Singh Committee recommended the insertion of Part XIV-A into the Constitution.
Appeals against Administrative Tribunal orders must first go to the Division Bench of the High Court, not directly to the Supreme Court (L. Chandra Kumar Case, 1997).
